answers.working:
A **proton gradient** across the thylakoid membrane means more \(\mathrm{H^+}\) inside the lumen than in the stroma. Three events build it up.

(i) When plastoquinone carries electrons from PS II towards the cytochrome complex, it releases protons into the lumen. (ii) The NADP reductase sits on the stroma side, so reducing \(\mathrm{NADP^+}\) to \(\mathrm{NADPH + H^+}\) uses up protons from the stroma, lowering the stroma's proton count. (iv) Splitting of water happens on the lumen side of PS II, so the protons it releases stay in the lumen.

Statement (iii) is wrong: ATP synthase does not pump protons into the lumen. It lets protons flow OUT of the lumen into the stroma, and this flow (which reduces the gradient) drives ATP formation.

So the answer is option (C).

Recall the vascular arrangement in each organ.

- **Dicot root**: xylem and phloem on different radii (radial), cambium forms later so open, with 2 to 4 xylem bundles (diarch to tetrarch). P matches (i).
- **Dicot stem**: bundles arranged in a ring, xylem and phloem together on the same radius (conjoint) with cambium between them (open). Q matches (ii).
- **Monocot root**: radial, no cambium (closed), many xylem bundles (polyarch). R matches (iii).
- **Monocot stem**: bundles scattered in the ground tissue, conjoint and without cambium (closed). S matches (iv).

So the answer is option (D).

answers.value: Q is a predator of P
answers.working:
Read the graphs in pairs. Grown alone, both P and Q rise and level off at a steady number, so each can survive on its own. Grown together, Q still rises to about the same level, but P rises for a while, peaks and then falls to zero.

So living together **harms P** and does not harm Q. Check each option against this.

- Commensalism (B) would leave P unaffected, but P is wiped out.
- Mutualism (C) would help both, but P is harmed.
- If P were a parasite of Q (D), P would gain and Q would suffer, which is the opposite of what is seen.
- If Q is a predator of P (A), P is the one that is harmed and declines, while Q survives.

Only option (A) has P as the harmed partner and Q as the one not harmed. So the answer is option (A).

Note: as printed, Q grows just as well alone as with P, so the graphs also look like competitive exclusion (Q outcompeting P). Competition is not offered, and among the choices given only predation by Q fits.

answers.value: The cells with the recombinant plasmid can grow in the presence of ampicillin but not tetracycline
answers.working:
This is **insertional inactivation**. When the foreign DNA is inserted inside the tetracycline resistance gene, that gene is broken and no longer works. The ampicillin resistance gene is untouched.

So a cell carrying the **recombinant** plasmid is resistant to ampicillin but sensitive to tetracycline: it grows on ampicillin and not on tetracycline. This is option (D), and it rules out option (A).

A cell carrying the **non-recombinant** plasmid still has both genes intact, so it grows on both antibiotics. That makes options (B) and (C) wrong.

So the answer is option (D).

answers.value: Plot of velocity of reaction (V) against [S] with a dashed Vmax line at V = 16: V is 2.5 at [S] = 5, 5 at [S] = 10, 8 at [S] = 20, 12 at [S] = 40, about 15.5 at [S] = 60, and 16 from [S] = 80 to 150
answers.working:
The **Michaelis constant** \(K_m\) is the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of its maximum, \(V_{max}/2\).

In every plot \(V_{max} = 16\), so we need the plot where \(V = 16/2 = 8\) at \([S] = 20\).

- Plot (A): at \([S] = 20\), \(V\) is only about 4; it reaches 8 at about \([S] = 36\).
- Plot (B): \(V = 8\) at \([S] = 40\), so \(K_m = 40\).
- Plot (C): \(V = 8\) at \([S] = 20\), so \(K_m = 20\).
- Plot (D): \(V = 8\) already at \([S] = 5\), so \(K_m = 5\).

So the answer is option (C).

answers.value: FSH interacts with membrane-bound receptor and generates cyclic AMP, while estrogen interacts with intracellular receptor and regulates gene expression
answers.working:
FSH is a **protein (glycoprotein) hormone**. It cannot cross the cell membrane, so it binds a receptor on the cell surface. This produces a **second messenger** such as cyclic AMP inside the cell, which changes the cell's metabolism.

Estrogen is a **steroid hormone**. Being lipid soluble, it passes through the membrane and binds an intracellular (nuclear) receptor. The hormone and receptor together act on the DNA and change gene expression.

Option (D) swaps the two, and options (A) and (B) wrongly give both hormones the same mechanism.

So the answer is option (C).

answers.working:
**Mycoplasma** is the only common organism with **no cell wall** at all.

If the cell wall were the only basis for classification, Mycoplasma would go with the group whose members lack a cell wall. Fungi have a chitin cell wall and plants a cellulose cell wall, and many protists have cell walls or walled stages. Animal cells have no cell wall.

So Mycoplasma would be grouped with animals, and the answer is option (D).

answers.working:
First find the direction of transcription. The promoter is on the right and the arrow at the transcription start site points to the **left**, so RNA is made moving from right to left, towards the terminator.

RNA is always made \(5' \to 3'\), so the **template strand** must be read \(3' \to 5'\) in that same leftward direction. The top strand runs 5' on the left and 3' on the right, so moving leftwards along it goes \(3' \to 5'\). The top strand is therefore the template.

The **coding strand** is the other (bottom) strand. It reads, left to right, 3'-CACTTCGGCAATGTCGTG-5'. Written in the usual \(5' \to 3'\) direction (right to left), this is 5'-GTGCTGTAACGGCTTCAC-3'. Its sequence matches the RNA, with T in place of U.

Option (B) is the template strand and option (D) is the coding strand written backwards. So the answer is option (C).

answers.value: Increase of \(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\) in sarcoplasm, unmasking of active sites for myosin, 'Z' lines pulled inwards
answers.working:
Acetylcholine produces an action potential in the muscle fibre, and this causes the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release calcium. So \(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\) in the sarcoplasm **increases**.

\(\mathrm{Ca^{++}}\) binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin and **unmasks the active sites** on actin for myosin. The myosin heads then form cross bridges and pull the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, so the 'Z' lines are pulled **inwards** and the sarcomere shortens.

Option (A) has a decrease in calcium, option (B) has the Z lines moving outwards, and option (D) masks the sites. So the answer is option (C).

answers.value: Anti-Rh antibody to the Rh-negative mother after delivery of the first Rh-positive child
answers.working:
**Erythroblastosis foetalis** happens when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby. During the first delivery some of the baby's Rh-positive blood enters the mother, and she starts making anti-Rh antibodies. In the next Rh-positive pregnancy these antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the baby's red blood cells.

It is prevented by giving the **Rh-negative mother** anti-Rh antibodies right after the delivery of her **first Rh-positive child**. These destroy the baby's Rh antigens before her own immune system can respond, so she never becomes sensitised.

An Rh-positive mother never makes anti-Rh antibodies, and an Rh-negative baby does not sensitise an Rh-negative mother, so options (B), (C) and (D) are not cases where the treatment is needed. So the answer is option (A).

answers.working:
In **negative regulation** of the lac operon, the regulator gene i makes a repressor all the time from its own promoter. The repressor binds the **operator**, which lies between the operon's promoter and the structural genes, and stops their transcription. So we need: an i gene with its own promoter, then promoter, operator, and the structural genes after the operator.

- (i) P, i, P, O, z, y, a: exactly this layout. Correct.
- (iii) P, i, P, O, y, z, a: the same layout with y and z swapped. All three genes are still after the operator, so they are still switched off by the repressor. Correct.
- (ii) P, O, i, z, P, y, a: y and a have their own promoter with no operator, so they are made all the time and are not regulated.
- (iv) P, O, i, P, z, y, a: z, y and a are transcribed from a promoter with no operator, so the repressor cannot stop them.

So the answer is option (B).

Work out the children in each case.

- (A) AB \(\times\) A (\(I^AI^A\) or \(I^Ai\)): children can be A, AB or B, so some match a parent.
- (B) AB (\(I^AI^B\)) \(\times\) O (\(ii\)): children are \(I^Ai\) or \(I^Bi\), that is group A or group B only. None can be AB or O.
- (C) A \(\times\) O: children are A or O, the same as a parent.
- (D) O \(\times\) B: children are B or O, the same as a parent.

Only in (B) is every child different from both parents. So the answer is option (B).

**RNA interference (RNAi)** is started by a **double-stranded RNA**. The cell cuts it into small pieces, and these bind the matching mRNA and silence it.

Check the options. Option (A) is single-stranded DNA (it has T). Option (B) is RNA (it has U) but single-stranded. Option (D) is double-stranded but it is DNA (both strands have T). Option (C) is RNA, and its two strands pair base for base (A with U, G with C), so it is a double-stranded RNA.

So the answer is option (C).

answers.label: D
answers.working:
Look at what the affected **fathers** pass on. The affected man in generation I has three daughters, all affected, and three sons, none affected. In generation IV, each of the two affected men again has all daughters affected and all sons unaffected. A father gives his X to every daughter and never to a son, so this is the hallmark of an **X-linked dominant** trait.

The affected mothers (the two affected daughters in generation II) pass the trait to about half their sons and half their daughters, which also fits X-linked dominant inheritance.

It cannot be Y-linked (affected men have no affected sons), and it is not mitochondrial (it passes through affected fathers). If it were X-linked recessive, the daughters of an affected man and an unaffected woman would be carriers, not affected. So the answer is option (D).

During foetal development, oogonia multiply and enter meiosis I to form **primary oocytes**. These oocytes stop partway through the first meiotic division, in **prophase I**, and stay arrested there.

No new oogonia are formed after birth, so a baby girl is born with all her primary oocytes held in prophase I. Meiosis I is completed only at puberty, just before ovulation, when a secondary oocyte is formed.

So the answer is option (B).
